title: The Ownership Checklist
story: Internalize the ownership model — once you do, bugs become impossible. A senior developer who mastered Rust's ownership reported: 'I haven't had a segfault in 5 years. When I go back to C++, I literally can't write unsafe code anymore — my brain rejects it.'
why: Systematically tracing ownership for every variable eliminates entire categories of memory bugs before they reach the compiler.
analogy: The ownership checklist is like a pilot's pre-flight checklist — boring, repetitive, and the reason planes almost never crash.
try_it: Write a function that takes ownership of a Score (by value), calls read_score on it, then returns the Score. Then in main, create a Score, pass it by value, receive it back, and read it again. Trace the ownership at each step.
tips: Print the three questions on a sticky note and put it on your monitor for the first week
When you get a borrow checker error, apply the checklist — the answer is almost always in Q2 or Q3
Contracts are the 4th question: 'Does the requires hold? Will the ensures be satisfied?'
common_mistakes: Forgetting that move transfers ownership — after `fn take(x: Data)`, the caller can't use x
Assuming `clone()` is implicit — XIOM never clones automatically; you must call `.clone()`
Skipping the checklist 'because this function is simple' — the simple ones are where complacency bites
